Unit 10 — Bayesian Thinking and Probabilistic Reasoning

Frequentist statistics answers “how surprising would these data be if nothing were going on?”. Bayesian statistics answers the question researchers actually ask — “given these data, what should I now believe?” — at the price of having to say what you believed beforehand. This unit is the one place in the course where that price is paid explicitly, and it is worth paying whenever the data are small, nested, or arriving one experiment at a time: a thesis project with three replicas, a compound measured in two assays, a screening campaign whose hit rate must be estimated after forty tested molecules. We build the machinery from arithmetic upwards — Bayes’ theorem on natural frequencies, conjugate updating by hand, grid approximation, and a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler written from scratch in fifteen lines — and apply it to two problems the laboratory meets constantly: what is the probability that a predicted hit is really active, and how should potencies measured in 108 different assays be combined. The second question introduces partial pooling, the single most useful idea in this unit, and the R edition cross-checks the hand-written sampler against lme4’s mixed model.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad (optativa, recomendada para proyectos con datos escasos o con estructura jerárquica) presenta el razonamiento bayesiano. Se enuncia el teorema de Bayes en palabras y se aplica a la falacia de la tasa base: dada una prevalencia y un factor de enriquecimiento, ¿cuál es la probabilidad de que un “hit” computacional sea realmente activo? Se realiza la actualización conjugada beta-binomial a mano, la aproximación por malla y un muestreador de Metropolis escrito desde cero, con diagnósticos de convergencia (trazas, R-hat, tamaño efectivo de muestra). Se ajusta un modelo jerárquico de la potencia frente a ROCK1 en 108 ensayos que muestra el encogimiento (shrinkage) de las medias de los ensayos pequeños hacia la media global, y se contrasta con el ajuste de efectos mixtos de lme4::lmer. Se realizan comprobaciones predictivas previas y posteriores, y se comparan intervalos creíbles e intervalos de confianza sobre los mismos datos. Nota: no se usa ningún lenguaje de programación probabilística; todos los modelos se implementan explícitamente, que es el objetivo pedagógico.

Learning objectives

  • State Bayes’ theorem in words and apply it to diagnostic-test and virtual-screening scenarios, including the base-rate fallacy.
  • Build and interpret simple Bayesian models — beta–binomial, normal with unknown mean — and read a posterior and a credible interval.
  • Compute a posterior three ways: conjugate algebra, grid approximation and Markov chain Monte Carlo.
  • Write a Metropolis sampler from scratch and diagnose it with trace plots, acceptance rate, R-hat and effective sample size.
  • Explain hierarchical (partial-pooling) models, why they suit compounds nested in assays or frames nested in replicas, and what shrinkage does.
  • Run prior and posterior predictive checks and justify a prior to a referee.
  • State the difference between a credible interval and a confidence interval, and when the two coincide.

How to read this unit

Read linearly, running each chunk; then change a prior and re-run, which is the fastest way to develop intuition for how much the prior actually matters. Everything here runs on base R’s stats[1] plus data.table, ggplot2, Matrix for the frozen fingerprints and lme4[2] for the mixed-model cross-check of §9; in a fresh Google Colab R runtime run once: install.packages(c(“data.table”,“ggplot2”,“Matrix”,“lme4”,“R.utils”)). No probabilistic-programming library is required or used: every model is implemented explicitly, which is the teaching point. This unit is marked extended: it assumes Unit 7 and Unit 8, and it pairs with Unit 9, whose mixed-effects model is the frequentist sibling of §7. 

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(Matrix); library(lme4)
})
set.seed(0)
PAL <- c(blue = "#2b5d9b", orange = "#d2691e", green = "#3a7d44", purple = "#6a4c93")
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
          theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)))
D <- function(f) file.path("..", "data", f)
cat("R", paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
    "| data.table", as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
    "| ggplot2", as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")),
    "| lme4", as.character(packageVersion("lme4")), "\n")
## R 4.5.3 | data.table 1.18.6.1 | ggplot2 4.0.3 | lme4 2.0.6

1. Bayes’ theorem in words

For a hypothesis \(H\) and data \(D\),

\[\underbrace{P(H\mid D)}_{\text{posterior}} = \frac{\overbrace{P(D\mid H)}^{\text{likelihood}}\;\overbrace{P(H)}^{\text{prior}}}{\underbrace{P(D)}_{\text{evidence}}},\]

which in words is: what you should believe after seeing the data is what the data say about each hypothesis, weighted by what you believed before, renormalised. The denominator is just the sum of the numerator over all hypotheses, so it rarely needs separate attention.

Three consequences are worth internalising before any computation:

  1. The likelihood alone is not enough. \(P(D\mid H)\) and \(P(H\mid D)\) are different quantities, and confusing them is the formal content of the base-rate fallacy (§2) and of the commonest misreading of a p-value[3][4].
  2. The prior is an assumption, like every other modelling choice, and it must be stated, justified and varied in a sensitivity analysis (§5). A model with no prior is not assumption-free; it has made a hidden one.
  3. The output is a distribution, not a number. Everything a Bayesian analysis reports — a point estimate, an interval, a probability that one series is more potent than another — is a summary of that distribution.

Domain context — virtual screening, prevalence and enrichment

A virtual screen ranks a large library of purchasable molecules with a computational score and sends the top fraction — typically the best 0.1 % to 1 % — for experimental testing. Two numbers describe how well it worked. The prevalence (or base rate) is the proportion of genuinely active molecules in the library; for a real vendor catalogue screened against one target it is of the order of 0.01 % to 1 %. The enrichment factor at x %, EFx%, is the hit rate among the selected top x % divided by the prevalence: an EF of 10 means the screen found ten times more actives than picking at random would have[5]. Note the ceiling: EF cannot exceed 1/prevalence, since the hit rate cannot exceed 1. The decoys used to measure enrichment in a benchmark are molecules presumed inactive, and how they were chosen changes every number[6] — the subject of Unit 19. The quantity a medicinal chemist actually needs is none of these: it is the probability that a molecule the computer selected will turn out to be active, which is a posterior probability and is computed below.

2. The base-rate fallacy, with natural frequencies

The classic demonstration is medical. A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test detects 99 % of cases and gives a false positive in 5 % of healthy people. Your test is positive. What is the probability that you are ill?

The intuitive answer is “about 95 %”. The correct answer is obtained by counting people rather than manipulating probabilities[7]:

ill healthy total
test positive 99 4,995 5,094
test negative 1 94,905 94,906
total 100 99,900 100,000

Of 100,000 people, 100 are ill; the test finds 99 of them. Of the 99,900 healthy people, 5 % — 4,995 — also test positive. So among the 5,094 positive tests only 99 are genuinely ill: P(ill | positive) = 99/5,094 ≈ 1.9 %. The test is excellent and the posterior is still under 2 %, because the prior was 0.1 %. Physicians asked this question answer it wrongly at a famously high rate[8].

The virtual-screening problem has exactly the same arithmetic, with prevalence in place of disease frequency and the enrichment factor in place of sensitivity and specificity. If selecting the top x % of a library enriches actives by a factor EF, then by definition

\[P(\text{active}\mid\text{selected}) = \mathrm{EF}_{x\%}\times \text{prevalence}.\]

N <- 100000; prev_med <- 0.001; sens <- 0.99; fpr <- 0.05
ill <- N * prev_med
tab <- matrix(c(ill * sens, ill * (1 - sens), (N - ill) * fpr, (N - ill) * (1 - fpr)), nrow = 2,
              dimnames = list(c("test positive", "test negative"), c("ill", "healthy")))
tab <- cbind(tab, total = rowSums(tab))
print(tab)
##               ill healthy total
## test positive  99    4995  5094
## test negative   1   94905 94906
cat(sprintf("\nP(ill | positive) = %d / %d = %.4f  (%.1f %%)\n\n",
            tab[1, "ill"], tab[1, "total"], tab[1, "ill"] / tab[1, "total"],
            100 * tab[1, "ill"] / tab[1, "total"]))
## 
## P(ill | positive) = 99 / 5094 = 0.0194  (1.9 %)
prevs <- 10^seq(-4, -0.3, length.out = 200)
curves <- rbindlist(lapply(c(3, 10, 30, 100), function(ef)
  data.table(ef = factor(sprintf("EF = %d", ef), levels = sprintf("EF = %d", c(3, 10, 30, 100))),
             prevalence = prevs, p_active = pmin(1, ef * prevs))))
p <- ggplot(curves, aes(prevalence, p_active, colour = ef)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "prevalence of actives in the library (log scale)", y = "P(active | selected by the screen)",
       title = "Even a tenfold enrichment leaves most picks inactive")
print(p)

scen <- data.table(scenario = c("focused library, strong model", "curated subset", "vendor catalogue",
                                "vendor catalogue, excellent model"),
                   prevalence = c(0.20, 0.01, 0.001, 0.001), EF = c(3, 10, 10, 100))
scen[, `P(active | selected)` := pmin(1, prevalence * EF)]
scen[, `actives among 100 ordered` := round(100 * `P(active | selected)`, 1)]
knitr::kable(scen, digits = 4)
scenario prevalence EF P(active | selected) actives among 100 ordered
focused library, strong model 0.200 3 0.60 60
curated subset 0.010 10 0.10 10
vendor catalogue 0.001 10 0.01 1
vendor catalogue, excellent model 0.001 100 0.10 10

Figure 1. Posterior probability that a selected molecule is active, as a function of the library’s prevalence of actives, for four enrichment factors. The curves are straight lines on these axes because the posterior is simply EF × prevalence until it saturates at 1. At a realistic catalogue prevalence of 0.1 %, even an enrichment factor of 10 gives a 1 % chance that any individual pick is active — one hit per hundred compounds ordered — and an enrichment of 100, which would be an outstanding result, gives one in ten. The table below the figure converts the same arithmetic into compounds ordered.

This single calculation explains several things students find puzzling. It explains why experimental groups ask for 50–100 compounds from a virtual screen rather than 5: at a 1–10 % expected hit rate, ordering five compounds has a substantial chance of returning nothing. It explains why benchmark enrichment factors are optimistic: a benchmark set has a prevalence of several per cent by construction (ours is 10.9 %), a hundred times higher than a real catalogue. And it is structurally the same calculation as the positive predictive value of a significant p-value[4][3]: a “significant” result from a field in which few hypotheses are true is mostly a false positive, for exactly the reason the medical table above is mostly false positives.

Substitution in the R edition — fingerprints

The ligand-based score below is the maximum Tanimoto similarity of each library molecule to 25 reference actives. R has no RDKit binding in this environment, so the Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits) are loaded from the frozen sparse file data/screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz and rebuilt with Matrix::sparseMatrix(), exactly as in Unit 8; the provenance is in data/manifest_fingerprints.json and the structures ship as data/rock1_curated.sdf.gz for anyone who wants to recompute them with ChemmineR. 

lib <- fread(D("screening_library.csv"))
fp  <- fread(D("screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz"))
M   <- sparseMatrix(i = match(fp$id, lib$inchikey), j = fp$bit + 1L, x = 1, dims = c(nrow(lib), 2048))
pc  <- rowSums(M)
set.seed(0)
ref <- sample(which(lib$label == 1), 25)
inter <- as.matrix(M %*% t(M[ref, , drop = FALSE]))
score <- apply(inter / (outer(pc, pc[ref], "+") - inter), 1, max)
keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(lib)); keep[ref] <- FALSE
s_lib <- score[keep]; y_lib <- lib$label[keep]
prev_bench <- mean(y_lib)
cat(sprintf("benchmark prevalence of actives: %.3f -> maximum possible EF = 1/prevalence = %.1f\n",
            prev_bench, 1 / prev_bench))
## benchmark prevalence of actives: 0.109 -> maximum possible EF = 1/prevalence = 9.2
for (frac in c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)) {
  top <- order(-s_lib)[1:floor(frac * length(s_lib))]
  cat(sprintf("  top %5.1f %% : hit rate %.3f -> EF = %.2f\n",
              100 * frac, mean(y_lib[top]), mean(y_lib[top]) / prev_bench))
}
##   top   1.0 % : hit rate 1.000 -> EF = 9.21
##   top   5.0 % : hit rate 1.000 -> EF = 9.21
##   top  10.0 % : hit rate 0.868 -> EF = 8.00
##   top  20.0 % : hit rate 0.475 -> EF = 4.38
ef10 <- mean(y_lib[order(-s_lib)[1:floor(0.10 * length(s_lib))]]) / prev_bench
for (pr in c(0.10, 0.01, 0.001))
  cat(sprintf("if the real library had prevalence %.3f, this EF of %.2f gives P(active|pick) = %.4f\n",
              pr, ef10, min(1, ef10 * pr)))
## if the real library had prevalence 0.100, this EF of 8.00 gives P(active|pick) = 0.7997
## if the real library had prevalence 0.010, this EF of 8.00 gives P(active|pick) = 0.0800
## if the real library had prevalence 0.001, this EF of 8.00 gives P(active|pick) = 0.0080

The ranking is genuinely good — at the top 1 % and even the top 5 % every selected molecule is an active, which is the maximum the benchmark allows, since the enrichment factor is capped at 1/prevalence = 9.2. That cap is the first thing to check when reading an enrichment number in a paper: an EF of 9.2 on a benchmark with 10.9 % actives is a perfect result, while the same screen applied to a catalogue with 0.1 % actives would still return 99 inactive compounds in every 100 ordered (P(active | pick) = 0.008 at EF 8.0).

3. The beta–binomial, by hand

The simplest real Bayesian model: we test \(n\) compounds from a screen, \(k\) turn out active, and we want the posterior for the hit rate \(\theta\).

  • Likelihood: \(P(k \mid \theta) \propto \theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}\) — the binomial.
  • Prior: \(\theta \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)\), whose density is proportional to \(\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\). Beta(1,1) is uniform; Beta(2,18) has mean 0.1 and is the sort of weakly informative prior a chemist’s experience justifies.
  • Posterior: multiplying, \(\theta \mid k \sim \text{Beta}(a+k,\; b+n-k)\). The prior is conjugate: the posterior is in the same family, and updating is addition.

Worked example

Prior Beta(2, 18) — “we expect about 10 % hits, with the confidence of about 20 prior observations”. We test 40 compounds and 6 are active.

Posterior = Beta(2 + 6, 18 + 40 − 6) = Beta(8, 52).

quantity formula value
prior mean a/(a+b) = 2/20 0.1000
maximum-likelihood estimate k/n = 6/40 0.1500
posterior mean 8/(8+52) 0.1333
posterior mode (8−1)/(8+52−2) = 7/58 0.1207
posterior SD √(ab/((a+b)²(a+b+1))) with a=8, b=52 0.0435

The posterior mean sits between the prior mean and the data estimate, closer to the data because 40 observations outweigh the 20 observations’ worth of prior. That compromise is the whole of Bayesian updating, and it is also the mechanism behind the shrinkage of §7.

a0 <- 2; b0 <- 18; n_tested <- 40; k_active <- 6
a1 <- a0 + k_active; b1 <- b0 + n_tested - k_active
cat(sprintf("prior Beta(%d, %d): mean %.4f\n", a0, b0, a0 / (a0 + b0)))
## prior Beta(2, 18): mean 0.1000
cat(sprintf("data: %d active out of %d -> MLE %.4f\n", k_active, n_tested, k_active / n_tested))
## data: 6 active out of 40 -> MLE 0.1500
cat(sprintf("posterior Beta(%d, %d): mean %.4f, mode %.4f, sd %.4f\n", a1, b1, a1 / (a1 + b1),
            (a1 - 1) / (a1 + b1 - 2), sqrt(a1 * b1 / ((a1 + b1)^2 * (a1 + b1 + 1)))))
## posterior Beta(8, 52): mean 0.1333, mode 0.1207, sd 0.0435
cat(sprintf("95 %% credible interval (equal-tailed): [%.4f, %.4f]\n", qbeta(0.025, a1, b1), qbeta(0.975, a1, b1)))
## 95 % credible interval (equal-tailed): [0.0604, 0.2293]
cat(sprintf("P(hit rate > 0.10 | data) = %.3f\n", pbeta(0.10, a1, b1, lower.tail = FALSE)))
## P(hit rate > 0.10 | data) = 0.766
cat(sprintf("P(hit rate > 0.20 | data) = %.3f\n", pbeta(0.20, a1, b1, lower.tail = FALSE)))
## P(hit rate > 0.20 | data) = 0.075
th <- seq(0, 0.6, length.out = 500)
lik <- dbinom(k_active, n_tested, th); lik <- lik / (sum(lik) * diff(th)[1])
dens <- rbind(data.table(theta = th, d = dbeta(th, a0, b0), what = "prior Beta(2, 18)"),
              data.table(theta = th, d = lik, what = "likelihood (6 of 40), normalised"),
              data.table(theta = th, d = dbeta(th, a1, b1), what = "posterior Beta(8, 52)"))
band <- data.table(theta = th[th >= qbeta(0.025, a1, b1) & th <= qbeta(0.975, a1, b1)])
band[, d := dbeta(theta, a1, b1)]
p <- ggplot(dens, aes(theta, d, colour = what)) +
  geom_area(data = band, aes(theta, d), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = PAL["orange"], alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("green", "blue", "orange")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "hit rate theta", y = "density",
       title = "Prior x likelihood = posterior, with the 95 % credible interval shaded")
print(p)

Figure 2. The three densities of a Bayesian update. The prior (blue) is broad and centred at 0.10; the normalised likelihood (green) is centred at the data estimate 0.15 and is wider still, because 40 observations do not pin down a proportion tightly; the posterior (orange) is narrower than either and sits at 0.1333, between them. The shaded region is the 95 % credible interval, 0.060 to 0.229. Note what the posterior lets us say directly: the probability that the true hit rate exceeds 10 % is 0.766, and that it exceeds 20 % is 0.075 — statements about the parameter, which a confidence interval is not allowed to make (§10). 

true_rate <- 0.12
set.seed(0)
outcomes <- runif(400) < true_rate
seqs <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0, 10, 40, 120, 400), function(n_seen) {
  k <- sum(outcomes[seq_len(n_seen)])
  data.table(theta = th, d = dbeta(th, a0 + k, b0 + n_seen - k),
             what = sprintf("after %d tested (%d active)", n_seen, k))
}))
seqs[, what := factor(what, levels = unique(what))]
ns <- 1:400; ks <- cumsum(outcomes)
run <- data.table(n = ns, mean = (a0 + ks) / (a0 + b0 + ns), mle = ks / ns,
                  lo = qbeta(0.025, a0 + ks, b0 + ns - ks), hi = qbeta(0.975, a0 + ks, b0 + ns - ks))
p1 <- ggplot(seqs, aes(theta, d, colour = what)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_rate, linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.4)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey70", unname(PAL)), name = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(7, "pt")) +
  labs(x = "hit rate theta", y = "density", title = "the posterior concentrates")
p2 <- ggplot(run, aes(n)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL["blue"], alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mle), colour = PAL["green"], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_rate, linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.35)) +
  labs(x = "compounds tested", y = "hit rate",
       title = "the prior washes out (band: 95 % CrI; green: k/n)")
print(p1); print(p2)

for (n_seen in c(5, 20, 100, 400)) {
  k <- sum(outcomes[1:n_seen])
  cat(sprintf("after %3d tested, %3d active: MLE %.3f | posterior mean %.3f | 95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
              n_seen, k, k / n_seen, (a0 + k) / (a0 + b0 + n_seen),
              qbeta(0.025, a0 + k, b0 + n_seen - k), qbeta(0.975, a0 + k, b0 + n_seen - k)))
}
## after   5 tested,   0 active: MLE 0.000 | posterior mean 0.080 | 95% CrI [0.010, 0.211]
## after  20 tested,   1 active: MLE 0.050 | posterior mean 0.075 | 95% CrI [0.016, 0.173]
## after 100 tested,   8 active: MLE 0.080 | posterior mean 0.083 | 95% CrI [0.041, 0.139]
## after 400 tested,  37 active: MLE 0.092 | posterior mean 0.093 | 95% CrI [0.067, 0.122]

Figure 3. Left: the posterior after 0, 10, 40, 120 and 400 tested compounds, with the true rate of 0.12 dashed. Right: the posterior mean with its credible band against the running maximum-likelihood estimate (green). Two features matter. The maximum-likelihood estimate is wild at small n — after five compounds it is exactly 0 here, which no one believes — while the posterior mean is pulled towards the prior and gives 0.080 with an interval of 0.010 to 0.211. And the prior’s influence decays: after 400 compounds (37 active) the posterior mean is 0.093 against a maximum-likelihood estimate of 0.092, indistinguishable, because 400 observations swamp 20 observations’ worth of prior belief.

This is the general answer to “but isn’t the prior arbitrary?”. A prior worth 20 observations matters when you have 5 and is irrelevant when you have 400. The honest practice is to say how much information your prior carries, and to check (§5) that the conclusion does not depend on it.

4. Grid approximation: Bayes without algebra

Conjugate priors are convenient and rare. The general method that always works in one or two dimensions is grid approximation: lay a grid over the parameter, evaluate prior × likelihood at every grid point, and normalise. It is the numerical definition of Bayes’ theorem, and it makes the mathematics unnecessary.

grid <- seq(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4, length.out = 1000)
dx <- diff(grid)[1]
lp <- dbeta(grid, a0, b0, log = TRUE) + dbinom(k_active, n_tested, grid, log = TRUE)
w <- exp(lp - max(lp)); w <- w / (sum(w) * dx)
cdf <- cumsum(w) * dx
cat(sprintf("grid vs analytic posterior mean: %.5f vs %.5f\n", sum(grid * w) * dx, a1 / (a1 + b1)))
## grid vs analytic posterior mean: 0.13333 vs 0.13333
cat(sprintf("grid vs analytic 95%% interval : [%.4f, %.4f] vs [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            grid[which.min(abs(cdf - 0.025))], grid[which.min(abs(cdf - 0.975))],
            qbeta(0.025, a1, b1), qbeta(0.975, a1, b1)))
## grid vs analytic 95% interval : [0.0601, 0.2293] vs [0.0604, 0.2293]
mix <- 0.7 * dbeta(grid, 2, 60) + 0.3 * dbeta(grid, 12, 20)      ## no conjugate partner exists
lp2 <- log(mix) + dbinom(k_active, n_tested, grid, log = TRUE)
w2 <- exp(lp2 - max(lp2)); w2 <- w2 / (sum(w2) * dx)
dd <- rbind(data.table(theta = grid, d = mix / (sum(mix) * dx), what = "bimodal prior (no conjugate form)"),
            data.table(theta = grid, d = w2, what = "posterior by grid approximation"),
            data.table(theta = grid, d = w, what = "posterior under the Beta(2,18) prior"))
p <- ggplot(dd, aes(theta, d, colour = what)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("green", "orange", "blue")]), name = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 6.5)) +
  labs(x = "hit rate theta", y = "density", title = "Grid approximation works for any prior you can write down")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("bimodal-prior posterior mean %.4f (vs %.4f under the conjugate prior)\n",
            sum(grid * w2) * dx, a1 / (a1 + b1)))
## bimodal-prior posterior mean 0.1409 (vs 0.1333 under the conjugate prior)
cat(sprintf("grid points: %d | cost: %d likelihood evaluations\n", length(grid), length(grid)))
## grid points: 1000 | cost: 1000 likelihood evaluations

Figure 4. Grid approximation. The blue curve reproduces the conjugate posterior of Figure 2 — the grid mean is 0.13333 against the analytic 0.13333, and the interval matches to three decimals — using nothing but 1,000 evaluations of prior × likelihood. The orange curve uses a deliberately awkward bimodal prior (green), a chemist who believes the campaign is either a dud or quite good, for which no conjugate update exists; the posterior is computed just as easily and ends up at 0.1409, slightly higher than the conjugate one.

Grid approximation is exact up to the grid resolution and completely transparent, which is why it is the right first tool. Its fatal limitation is dimensionality: a grid of 1,000 points per parameter costs 103 evaluations for one parameter, 106 for two and 109 for three. Beyond two or three parameters it is hopeless, and that is precisely the gap Markov chain Monte Carlo fills (§6).

5. How much does the prior matter?

The question a referee will ask is “would a different prior have changed your conclusion?”. The answer is obtained by refitting under several priors and tabulating — a prior sensitivity analysis, which costs three lines and should appear in every Bayesian paper.

priors <- list("uniform Beta(1,1)" = c(1, 1), "Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5)" = c(0.5, 0.5),
               "weak, 10 % Beta(2,18)" = c(2, 18), "strong, 10 % Beta(10,90)" = c(10, 90),
               "strong and wrong, 50 % Beta(50,50)" = c(50, 50))
k400 <- sum(outcomes)
sens <- rbindlist(lapply(names(priors), function(nm) {
  pp <- priors[[nm]]
  rbindlist(lapply(list(c(40, k_active), c(400, k400)), function(z) {
    n_ <- z[1]; k_ <- z[2]
    data.table(prior = nm, n_tested = n_, mean = (pp[1] + k_) / (sum(pp) + n_),
               lo = qbeta(0.025, pp[1] + k_, pp[2] + n_ - k_),
               hi = qbeta(0.975, pp[1] + k_, pp[2] + n_ - k_))
  }))
}))
sens[, prior := factor(prior, levels = rev(names(priors)))]

  labs(x = "posterior mean and 95 % credible interval for the hit rate", y = NULL,
       title = "Prior sensitivity: the data win if there are enough of them")
print(p)

Figure 5. Posterior means and credible intervals for five priors at two sample sizes (dashed line: the true rate of 0.12). With 40 compounds tested the five answers span 0.287 in the hit rate — the deliberately wrong Beta(50,50) prior drags the estimate to 0.400 against a maximum-likelihood value of 0.15 — and a reader is entitled to ask which prior was used. With 400 compounds the four defensible priors collapse onto 0.093–0.095, a spread of 0.002 among them, and only the strong, wrong prior remains visibly displaced at 0.174. The rule: report the sensitivity table, and if the conclusion changes across defensible priors, the data are not sufficient to support it.

Exercise 1

A collaborator insists on a Beta(1, 1) uniform prior “to avoid bias”. Compute the posterior for a campaign in which 0 of 12 compounds were active, under Beta(1,1), Beta(2,18) and Beta(0.5,0.5). Which prior gives the most defensible answer, and what does each imply about the probability that the true hit rate exceeds 20 %? (Note that the maximum-likelihood estimate here is exactly 0, with a Wald confidence interval that R’s own arithmetic reports as [0, 0] — see §10.)

6. Markov chain Monte Carlo, written from scratch

When the parameter space has more than two or three dimensions, we can no longer evaluate the posterior everywhere. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) instead constructs a random walk whose long-run visiting frequency is the posterior, so a histogram of the walk approximates the distribution. The Metropolis algorithm[9][10] is four lines:

  1. from the current position \(\theta\), propose \(\theta' = \theta + \text{noise}\);
  2. compute the ratio \(r = p(\theta'\mid D)/p(\theta\mid D)\) — note that the unknown normalising constant cancels, which is the trick that makes the whole thing possible;
  3. accept \(\theta'\) with probability \(\min(1, r)\), otherwise stay at \(\theta\);
  4. repeat, recording every position.

Modern samplers — Gibbs[11], Hamiltonian Monte Carlo[12] and the No-U-Turn sampler used by Stan and its R interfaces — are smarter about step 1, but the logic is identical.

log_posterior <- function(theta, a = a0, b = b0, n = n_tested, k = k_active) {
  if (theta <= 0 || theta >= 1) return(-Inf)
  dbeta(theta, a, b, log = TRUE) + dbinom(k, n, theta, log = TRUE)
}
metropolis <- function(log_p, start, step, n_iter, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  chain <- numeric(n_iter); theta <- start; lp <- log_p(theta); accepted <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    prop <- theta + rnorm(1, 0, step)
    lp_prop <- log_p(prop)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) { theta <- prop; lp <- lp_prop; accepted <- accepted + 1 }
    chain[i] <- theta
  }
  list(chain = chain, acceptance = accepted / n_iter)
}
chains <- lapply(1:4, function(i)
  metropolis(log_posterior, start = c(0.02, 0.10, 0.25, 0.45)[i], step = 0.15, n_iter = 8000, seed = i))
burn <- 1000
post_chains <- lapply(chains, function(z) z$chain[(burn + 1):8000])
pooled <- unlist(post_chains)
cat(sprintf("acceptance rates: %s  (0.2-0.5 is the healthy range for random-walk Metropolis)\n",
            paste(sprintf("%.3f", sapply(chains, `[[`, "acceptance")), collapse = ", ")))
## acceptance rates: 0.327, 0.325, 0.338, 0.320  (0.2-0.5 is the healthy range for random-walk Metropolis)
cat(sprintf("posterior mean  : MCMC %.4f vs analytic %.4f\n", mean(pooled), a1 / (a1 + b1)))
## posterior mean  : MCMC 0.1336 vs analytic 0.1333
cat(sprintf("95 %% interval   : MCMC [%.4f, %.4f] vs analytic [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            quantile(pooled, 0.025), quantile(pooled, 0.975), qbeta(0.025, a1, b1), qbeta(0.975, a1, b1)))
## 95 % interval   : MCMC [0.0598, 0.2299] vs analytic [0.0604, 0.2293]
rhat <- function(chs) {
  m <- do.call(rbind, chs); n <- ncol(m)
  W <- mean(apply(m, 1, var)); B <- n * var(rowMeans(m))
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}
ess <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  ac <- as.vector(acf(x, lag.max = min(1000, n - 1), plot = FALSE)$acf)
  stop_at <- which(ac < 0.05)[1]; if (is.na(stop_at)) stop_at <- length(ac)
  n / (1 + 2 * sum(ac[2:(stop_at - 1)]))
}

hist(pooled, breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = "grey80", border = NA, xlim = c(0, 0.4),

## R-hat (should be < 1.01): 1.0001

            paste(round(sapply(post_chains, ess)), collapse = ", "), length(post_chains[[1]])))
## effective sample size per chain: 1370, 1210, 1486, 1371  (of 7000 draws each)

            sd(pooled) / sqrt(sum(sapply(post_chains, ess)))))
## Monte-Carlo standard error of the posterior mean: 0.00059

Figure 6. Diagnosing a sampler. Left: the first 400 iterations of four chains started deliberately far apart at 0.02, 0.10, 0.25 and 0.45; all four reach the same region within roughly a hundred steps, and everything before the dashed line is discarded as burn-in. Centre: after burn-in the traces look like overlapping fuzzy caterpillars with no trends and no sticking — the visual signature of a healthy chain. Right: the pooled histogram lies under the analytic posterior, which is the strongest possible check since here we know the right answer: MCMC mean 0.1336 against the analytic 0.1333, interval [0.060, 0.230] against [0.060, 0.229].

Three numbers must accompany any MCMC result. The acceptance rate should be roughly 0.2–0.5 for a random-walk sampler (ours is 0.32–0.34); much lower means the steps are too large and the chain sticks, much higher means they are too small and it crawls. R-hat compares the variance between chains with the variance within them and should be below about 1.01[13][14]; ours is 1.0001. The effective sample size counts how many independent draws the autocorrelated chain is worth — 1,200 to 1,500 of 7,000 draws per chain here, which is exactly the quantity Unit 7 computed for molecular-dynamics frames, and for the same reason. Reporting a posterior without these is like reporting a simulation average without saying how long the trajectory was.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.6, 1), cex = 0.72)
step_rows <- rbindlist(lapply(list(c(0.005, 1), c(0.15, 2), c(1.00, 3)), function(z) {
  step <- z[1]
  cc <- lapply(1:4, function(i) metropolis(log_posterior, 0.15, step, 4000, seed = 100 + i))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 2000), ylim = c(0, 0.35), xlab = "iteration",
       ylab = if (z[2] == 1) "theta" else "",
       main = sprintf("step = %.3f (%s)", step, c("too small", "about right", "too large")[z[2]]))
  for (i in 1:4) lines(cc[[i]]$chain[1001:3000], col = adjustcolor(unname(PAL)[i], 0.8), lwd = 0.35)
  pcs <- lapply(cc, function(z2) z2$chain[1001:4000])
  data.table(step = step, acceptance = mean(sapply(cc, `[[`, "acceptance")), R_hat = rhat(pcs),
             ESS_per_chain = mean(sapply(pcs, ess)), posterior_mean = mean(unlist(pcs)))
}))

par(op)
cat(sprintf("analytic posterior mean %.4f\n\n", a1 / (a1 + b1)))
## analytic posterior mean 0.1333
knitr::kable(step_rows, digits = 4)
step acceptance R_hat ESS_per_chain posterior_mean
0.005 0.9697 1.0599 17.1176 0.1378
0.150 0.3328 1.0003 687.1352 0.1329
1.000 0.0543 1.0058 116.5822 0.1324

Figure 7. The same sampler at three step sizes. With steps that are too small (left) the chain accepts 97 % of proposals and drifts slowly, so the trace is a smooth wandering line rather than a caterpillar; with steps that are too large (right) only 5.4 % of proposals are accepted and the trace is a staircase of long flat sections. The middle panel is what a healthy chain looks like. The table gives the numbers, and they contain the warning: the posterior mean is within 0.005 of the analytic value in all three cases — which is exactly the danger — while the acceptance rate (0.970, 0.333, 0.054), R-hat (1.060, 1.000, 1.006) and effective sample size (17, 687, 117 per chain) separate them clearly. MCMC fails silently; the diagnostics are not optional.

7. Hierarchical models and shrinkage

Here is the problem this unit exists for. Our ROCK1 data come from many different assays, run in different laboratories with different protocols. Some assays measured hundreds of compounds, some measured three. What is “the” potency level of each assay?

Three possible answers:

  • Complete pooling — ignore the assay labels, use the grand mean for everything. Throws away real between-assay differences.
  • No pooling — estimate each assay separately. An assay with three measurements gets an estimate with an enormous standard error, and the most extreme-looking assays will mostly be the small ones.
  • Partial pooling — model the assay means as draws from a common distribution and let the data decide how much they differ. Each assay’s estimate is then a compromise between its own mean and the grand mean, weighted by how much information it carries.

Partial pooling is what a hierarchical model does. Formally, for measurement \(i\) in assay \(j\):

\[y_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta_j,\sigma^2),\qquad \theta_j\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\tau^2),\qquad \mu,\sigma,\tau \text{ given weakly informative priors.}\]

The posterior mean of \(\theta_j\) is approximately \(\lambda_j\bar y_j + (1-\lambda_j)\mu\) with \(\lambda_j = \tau^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j)\) — large assays keep their own mean, small assays are pulled towards the overall level. That pull is shrinkage, and it is not a Bayesian curiosity: it provably improves the average accuracy of the whole set of estimates[15], and it is the engine of the empirical-Bayes methods used throughout genomics[16][17].

raw <- fread(D("rock1_chembl_raw.csv"))
ok <- raw[standard_relation == "=" & !is.na(standard_value) &
          standard_units == "nM" & standard_value > 0]
ok[, pAct := 9 - log10(as.numeric(standard_value))]
ok <- ok[pAct > 2 & pAct < 12]
ok[, n_in_assay := .N, by = assay_chembl_id]
ok <- ok[n_in_assay >= 3]
ok[, code := .GRP, by = assay_chembl_id]
J <- uniqueN(ok$code); yobs <- ok$pAct; codes <- ok$code
nj <- as.numeric(table(codes)); ybar <- as.numeric(tapply(yobs, codes, mean))
assay_ids <- ok[, .(id = assay_chembl_id[1]), by = code][order(code)]$id
cat(sprintf("assays with at least 3 exact measurements : %d\n", J))
## assays with at least 3 exact measurements : 108
cat(sprintf("measurements used                         : %d\n", length(yobs)))
## measurements used                         : 3205
cat(sprintf("assay sizes: min %d, median %d, max %d\n", min(nj), median(nj), max(nj)))
## assay sizes: min 3, median 13, max 501
cat(sprintf("grand mean pActivity %.3f | SD of the %d assay means %.3f | pooled within-assay SD %.3f\n",
            mean(yobs), J, sd(ybar), sqrt(sum((yobs - ybar[codes])^2) / (length(yobs) - J))))
## grand mean pActivity 6.545 | SD of the 108 assay means 0.876 | pooled within-assay SD 0.828
cat(sprintf("the three smallest assays have means %s\n",
            paste(sprintf("%.3f", ybar[order(nj)][1:3]), collapse = ", ")))
## the three smallest assays have means 6.400, 6.233, 7.967
hierarchical_sampler <- function(seed, n_iter = 4000, burn = 1000) {
  set.seed(seed)
  mu <- 6.5; log_tau <- log(0.8); log_sig <- log(0.8); theta <- ybar; accepted <- 0
  keep <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_iter - burn, ncol = 3 + J)
  log_p_scales <- function(lt, ls, theta, mu) {
    ## HalfNormal(1) priors on tau and sigma, plus the log-Jacobian of the log transform
    t <- exp(lt); sg <- exp(ls)
    prior <- -0.5 * t^2 - 0.5 * sg^2 + lt + ls
    like  <- -J * lt - 0.5 * sum((theta - mu)^2) / t^2 -
             length(yobs) * ls - 0.5 * sum((yobs - theta[codes])^2) / sg^2
    prior + like
  }
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    tau <- exp(log_tau); sig <- exp(log_sig)
    prec  <- nj / sig^2 + 1 / tau^2                                   ## Gibbs step for every theta_j
    theta <- rnorm(J, (nj * ybar / sig^2 + mu / tau^2) / prec, 1 / sqrt(prec))
    mu    <- rnorm(1, mean(theta), tau / sqrt(J))                     ## Gibbs step for mu (flat prior)
    p_lt <- log_tau + rnorm(1, 0, 0.12); p_ls <- log_sig + rnorm(1, 0, 0.05)   ## Metropolis block
    if (log(runif(1)) < log_p_scales(p_lt, p_ls, theta, mu) - log_p_scales(log_tau, log_sig, theta, mu)) {
      log_tau <- p_lt; log_sig <- p_ls; accepted <- accepted + 1
    }
    if (it > burn) keep[it - burn, ] <- c(mu, exp(log_tau), exp(log_sig), theta)
  }
  list(draws = keep, acceptance = accepted / n_iter)
}
draws <- lapply(1:4, hierarchical_sampler)
post_h <- do.call(rbind, lapply(draws, `[[`, "draws"))
mu_post <- post_h[, 1]; tau_post <- post_h[, 2]; sig_post <- post_h[, 3]
theta_post <- post_h[, 4:(3 + J)]
cat(sprintf("acceptance rate of the Metropolis block: %s\n",
            paste(sprintf("%.3f", sapply(draws, `[[`, "acceptance")), collapse = ", ")))
## acceptance rate of the Metropolis block: 0.189, 0.189, 0.190, 0.194
cat(sprintf("R-hat  mu %.4f | tau %.4f | sigma %.4f\n",
            rhat(lapply(draws, function(d) d$draws[, 1])),
            rhat(lapply(draws, function(d) d$draws[, 2])),
            rhat(lapply(draws, function(d) d$draws[, 3]))))
## R-hat  mu 1.0000 | tau 1.0017 | sigma 1.0012
cat(sprintf("mu    (grand mean potency) %.3f  95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            mean(mu_post), quantile(mu_post, 0.025), quantile(mu_post, 0.975)))
## mu    (grand mean potency) 6.746  95% CrI [6.579, 6.915]
cat(sprintf("tau   (between-assay SD)   %.3f  95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            mean(tau_post), quantile(tau_post, 0.025), quantile(tau_post, 0.975)))
## tau   (between-assay SD)   0.843  95% CrI [0.728, 0.975]
cat(sprintf("sigma (within-assay SD)    %.3f  95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            mean(sig_post), quantile(sig_post, 0.025), quantile(sig_post, 0.975)))
## sigma (within-assay SD)    0.828  95% CrI [0.808, 0.849]

The sampler used 3,205 measurements from 108 assays whose sizes run from 3 to 501 compounds, and its Metropolis block accepted about 19 % of proposals — acceptable for a two-dimensional block, and R-hat is 1.002 or better for all three global parameters.

The two variance components are the scientific output of this model, and they answer a question the laboratory cares about. The within-assay standard deviation, 0.828 log units, is how much compounds differ inside one assay — real structure–activity variation plus measurement error. The between-assay standard deviation, 0.843 log units, is how much assays differ from each other after accounting for that: slightly larger, and the posterior probability that τ exceeds σ is 0.59, so the two sources of variation are of comparable size. That quantifies the warning of Unit 7 that potencies from different sources are not interchangeable[18][19]. The practical implication for any modelling project is that an assay label is a variable, not a nuisance.

theta_hat <- colMeans(theta_post)
theta_lo <- apply(theta_post, 2, quantile, 0.025)
theta_hi <- apply(theta_post, 2, quantile, 0.975)
