Figure 8. Left: each assay’s raw mean (orange) joined to its partially pooled posterior mean (blue), against the number of measurements. The assays on the left — three or four compounds each — are pulled substantially towards the grand mean of 6.75, by up to 0.466 log units; the assays on the right, with hundreds of measurements, do not move at all (0.001 and 0.002 log units for the two largest). Right: the size of the shift against assay size, with the theoretical (1 − λ) curve in orange; the agreement confirms that the sampler is doing what the algebra says. The mean shift for assays with five or fewer measurements, 0.151 log units, is nineteen times that for assays with fifty or more (0.008).

This figure is the argument for hierarchical modelling in one picture. The assay CHEMBL1099847, with three compounds averaging pActivity 7.967, is probably not a special assay; it is a small sample from the same population, and the model’s estimate of 7.667 is a better bet about its next compound than its own mean is. The same logic applies directly to the structures this group works with: frames nested in replicas (Unit 20), compounds nested in series, sites nested in patients (Unit 9’s blocking example). The frequentist counterpart is the mixed-effects model of §9 below; the Bayesian version additionally gives a full posterior for each group and for the variance components, which is what makes statements like “the probability that assay A is more sensitive than assay B is 0.83” available.

7.1 Does partial pooling actually predict better?

Shrinkage is justified by a claim about accuracy, so it should be tested rather than asserted. We hold out one measurement from each assay, fit all three strategies to the rest, and see which predicts the held-out values best.

set.seed(3)
held <- sapply(1:J, function(j) { idx <- which(codes == j); idx[sample(length(idx), 1)] })
train <- setdiff(seq_along(yobs), held)
nj_tr <- as.numeric(table(factor(codes[train], levels = 1:J)))
ybar_tr <- as.numeric(tapply(yobs[train], factor(codes[train], levels = 1:J), mean))
grand_tr <- mean(yobs[train])
tau_e <- mean(tau_post); sig_e <- mean(sig_post)
lam <- tau_e^2 / (tau_e^2 + sig_e^2 / pmax(nj_tr, 1))
partial <- lam * ybar_tr + (1 - lam) * grand_tr
pool_cmp <- rbindlist(lapply(list(list("complete pooling (grand mean)", rep(grand_tr, J)),
                                  list("no pooling (own assay mean)", ybar_tr),
                                  list("partial pooling (hierarchical)", partial)), function(z) {
  err <- yobs[held] - z[[2]]
  data.table(strategy = z[[1]], RMSE = sqrt(mean(err^2)), MAE = mean(abs(err)),
             `RMSE on assays with n<=5` = sqrt(mean(err[nj <= 5]^2)))
}))
cat(sprintf("held-out measurements: %d (one per assay) | training measurements: %d\n",
            length(held), length(train)))
## held-out measurements: 108 (one per assay) | training measurements: 3097
cat(sprintf("estimated shrinkage weight lambda: min %.2f (n=%d), max %.3f (n=%d)\n",
            min(lam), nj_tr[which.min(lam)], max(lam), nj_tr[which.max(lam)]))
## estimated shrinkage weight lambda: min 0.67 (n=2), max 0.998 (n=500)
knitr::kable(pool_cmp, digits = 4)
strategy RMSE MAE RMSE on assays with n<=5
complete pooling (grand mean) 1.1553 0.9298 1.1602
no pooling (own assay mean) 0.7345 0.5532 0.9950
partial pooling (hierarchical) 0.7333 0.5497 0.9587

Partial pooling wins on every column: held-out RMSE 0.7333 against 0.7345 for no pooling and 1.1553 for complete pooling, and the same ordering on mean absolute error. The margin over no pooling is small overall because most measurements belong to large assays, where the two strategies coincide — the shrinkage weight λ reaches 0.998 for the largest assay. The third column is where the difference lives: restricted to assays with five or fewer measurements, partial pooling (0.959) beats using the assay’s own mean (0.995), and both beat ignoring the labels (1.160). That is the argument in three numbers: with three measurements an assay mean is noisy enough that pulling it towards the grand mean improves the prediction, and the hierarchical model finds the right compromise without being told which regime it is in. This is a cross-validation of a Bayesian model, and it is the kind of evidence that persuades a referee who does not care about priors.

A posterior also answers questions a point estimate cannot, by simple counting over the draws.

ord <- order(-nj); a_idx <- ord[1]; b_idx <- ord[2]; small_idx <- order(nj)[1]
cat(sprintf("P(assay %s has higher mean potency than assay %s) = %.3f\n",
            assay_ids[a_idx], assay_ids[b_idx], mean(theta_post[, a_idx] > theta_post[, b_idx])))
## P(assay CHEMBL1963814 has higher mean potency than assay CHEMBL3889185) = 0.000
cat(sprintf("posterior mean difference %.3f log units, 95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            mean(theta_post[, a_idx] - theta_post[, b_idx]),
            quantile(theta_post[, a_idx] - theta_post[, b_idx], 0.025),
            quantile(theta_post[, a_idx] - theta_post[, b_idx], 0.975)))
## posterior mean difference -1.038 log units, 95% CrI [-1.153, -0.920]
cat(sprintf("P(the smallest assay, n=%d, has mean potency above 7) = %.3f  (its raw mean is %.3f)\n",
            nj[small_idx], mean(theta_post[, small_idx] > 7), ybar[small_idx]))
## P(the smallest assay, n=3, has mean potency above 7) = 0.105  (its raw mean is 6.400)
cat(sprintf("P(between-assay SD tau exceeds the within-assay SD sigma) = %.3f\n", mean(tau_post > sig_post)))
## P(between-assay SD tau exceeds the within-assay SD sigma) = 0.589
set.seed(5)
new_assay <- mu_post + tau_post * rnorm(length(mu_post))
cat(sprintf("posterior predictive for a NEW assay's mean: %.3f, 95%% CrI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            mean(new_assay), quantile(new_assay, 0.025), quantile(new_assay, 0.975)))
## posterior predictive for a NEW assay's mean: 6.744, 95% CrI [5.064, 8.452]

Each of these is a sentence a chemist can act on, obtained by counting draws rather than by consulting a table: the largest assay (501 compounds) sits 1.038 log units below the second largest (305 compounds), with a 95 % credible interval from −1.153 to −0.920 and a posterior probability of 0.000 that it is the more potent of the two — so the two are not interchangeable sources of training labels; the three-compound assay whose raw mean is 6.400 has only a 10.5 % posterior probability of being above pActivity 7; and an assay that has not been run yet would have a mean somewhere in 5.06 to 8.45 — a three-log-unit predictive interval, which is the honest summary of how heterogeneous this literature is. None of these statements has a frequentist counterpart that can be phrased as a probability about the quantity itself[30].

7.2 The three-replica problem, revisited

Units 7 and 8 left the molecular-dynamics comparison unresolved: three replicas per condition, a difference of 0.02 nm in mean C-alpha RMSD, p = 0.69, and an exact permutation test that could not have gone below 0.10. A Bayesian analysis cannot create information that the design did not collect — but it can state the result in a form that does not invite the wrong conclusion.

md_obs <- fread(D("md_trpcage_observables.csv"))
run_means <- md_obs[, .(m = mean(rmsd_ca_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)]
A <- run_means[condition == "A", m]; B <- run_means[condition == "B", m]
sd_rep <- sqrt((sum((A - mean(A))^2) + sum((B - mean(B))^2)) / (length(A) + length(B) - 2))
normal_posterior <- function(x, prior_mu = 0.20, prior_sd = 0.15, sd_known = sd_rep) {
  prec <- 1 / prior_sd^2 + length(x) / sd_known^2
  c(mean = (prior_mu / prior_sd^2 + sum(x) / sd_known^2) / prec, sd = 1 / sqrt(prec))
}
pa <- normal_posterior(A); pb <- normal_posterior(B)
set.seed(0)
diff_md <- rnorm(200000, pa["mean"], pa["sd"]) - rnorm(200000, pb["mean"], pb["sd"])
xs <- seq(0.02, 0.32, length.out = 400)
dd <- rbind(data.table(x = xs, d = dnorm(xs, pa["mean"], pa["sd"]), what = "300 K mean RMSD"),
            data.table(x = xs, d = dnorm(xs, pb["mean"], pb["sd"]), what = "340 K mean RMSD"))
p <- ggplot(dd, aes(x, d, colour = what)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = data.table(x = c(A, B), d = rep(c(0.3, 0.6), each = 3),
                               what = rep(c("300 K mean RMSD", "340 K mean RMSD"), each = 3)),
             size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "mean C-alpha RMSD (nm)", y = "posterior density",
       title = "Three replicas per condition: the posteriors overlap almost completely")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("replica SD (pooled, 4 df): %.4f nm\n", sd_rep))
## replica SD (pooled, 4 df): 0.0562 nm
cat(sprintf("300 K posterior mean %.4f, 95%% CrI [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            pa["mean"], pa["mean"] - 1.96 * pa["sd"], pa["mean"] + 1.96 * pa["sd"]))
## 300 K posterior mean 0.1748, 95% CrI [0.1127, 0.2369]
cat(sprintf("340 K posterior mean %.4f, 95%% CrI [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            pb["mean"], pb["mean"] - 1.96 * pb["sd"], pb["mean"] + 1.96 * pb["sd"]))
## 340 K posterior mean 0.1554, 95% CrI [0.0933, 0.2175]
cat(sprintf("difference: posterior mean %+.4f nm, 95%% CrI [%+.4f, %+.4f]\n",
            mean(diff_md), quantile(diff_md, 0.025), quantile(diff_md, 0.975)))
## difference: posterior mean +0.0193 nm, 95% CrI [-0.0685, +0.1070]
cat(sprintf("P(300 K is MORE mobile than 340 K) = %.3f   <- barely different from a coin flip\n",
            mean(diff_md > 0)))
## P(300 K is MORE mobile than 340 K) = 0.667   <- barely different from a coin flip
cat(sprintf("P(|difference| < 0.05 nm) = %.3f  <- the useful statement: any real effect is small\n",
            mean(abs(diff_md) < 0.05)))
## P(|difference| < 0.05 nm) = 0.693  <- the useful statement: any real effect is small

Figure 9. Posterior distributions for the mean C-alpha RMSD at each temperature, built from the three replica means per condition (dots) with a weakly informative Normal(0.20, 0.15) prior and the pooled replica SD of 0.0562 nm. The two posteriors overlap almost entirely. The posterior probability that the 300 K system is the more mobile one is 0.667 — leaning that way, but nowhere near a conclusion — while the probability that the two conditions differ by less than 0.05 nm is 0.693.

Compare the three available reports of the same experiment. The frequentist test says “p = 0.69, no significant difference”, which readers routinely misread as “no difference”. The exact permutation test says “p = 0.80, and 0.10 was the floor”, which is honest but conveys nothing about size. The Bayesian analysis says “the 300 K minus 340 K difference is +0.019 nm with a 95 % credible interval from −0.069 to +0.107, and the probability that it is smaller than 0.05 nm in magnitude is 0.69” — an explicit statement that the experiment has bounded the effect loosely rather than refuted it. That is the sentence to write in a thesis, and it is the clearest argument in this course for learning the Bayesian vocabulary even if the analysis itself stays frequentist[31].

For contrast, the next chunk runs the identical machinery on a comparison that is well powered — the two ROCK1 scaffold series of Unit 8 — so that the difference between “no evidence of an effect” and “evidence of no large effect” is visible side by side.

rock <- fread(D("rock1_chembl_curated.csv"))
ex_c <- rock[censored == FALSE]
cnt <- sort(table(ex_c$scaffold_smiles), decreasing = TRUE)
s1 <- ex_c[scaffold_smiles == names(cnt)[1], pActivity]
s2 <- ex_c[scaffold_smiles == names(cnt)[2], pActivity]
sd_pool <- sqrt(((length(s1) - 1) * var(s1) + (length(s2) - 1) * var(s2)) / (length(s1) + length(s2) - 2))
p1 <- normal_posterior(s1, 6.5, 2.0, sd_pool); p2 <- normal_posterior(s2, 6.5, 2.0, sd_pool)
set.seed(2)
d12 <- rnorm(200000, p1["mean"], p1["sd"]) - rnorm(200000, p2["mean"], p2["sd"])
cat(sprintf("series 1: n = %3d, mean %.3f | series 2: n = %2d, mean %.3f | pooled SD %.3f\n",
            length(s1), mean(s1), length(s2), mean(s2), sd_pool))
## series 1: n = 207, mean 7.397 | series 2: n = 59, mean 6.069 | pooled SD 0.858
cat(sprintf("posterior difference %+.3f log units, 95%% CrI [%+.3f, %+.3f]\n",
            mean(d12), quantile(d12, 0.025), quantile(d12, 0.975)))
## posterior difference +1.325 log units, 95% CrI [+1.078, +1.573]
cat(sprintf("P(series 1 more potent than series 2)      = %.4f\n", mean(d12 > 0)))
## P(series 1 more potent than series 2)      = 1.0000
cat(sprintf("P(the difference exceeds 1 log unit)       = %.4f\n", mean(d12 > 1)))
## P(the difference exceeds 1 log unit)       = 0.9949
cat(sprintf("P(the difference is smaller than 0.3 log)  = %.4f\n", mean(abs(d12) < 0.3)))
## P(the difference is smaller than 0.3 log)  = 0.0000
cat(sprintf("\nfor comparison, the MD replica question: P(difference > 0) = %.3f, P(|difference| < 0.05 nm) = %.3f\n",
            mean(diff_md > 0), mean(abs(diff_md) < 0.05)))
## 
## for comparison, the MD replica question: P(difference > 0) = 0.667, P(|difference| < 0.05 nm) = 0.693

With 207 and 59 compounds the posterior for the difference is tight and far from zero: series 1 is more potent with a probability indistinguishable from 1, the difference is +1.325 log units (95 % CrI 1.078 to 1.573), and the probability that it exceeds one log unit is 0.995. With three replicas per condition the posterior for the molecular-dynamics difference straddles zero and the probability of a positive difference is 0.667. Both analyses used the same three lines of code; what differs is the information in the data, which is precisely what a posterior is designed to display.

Exercise 2

Raise the lower bound on assay size from 3 to 10 measurements (ok[n_in_assay >= 10]) and re-run the sampler. Does the between-assay standard deviation tau go up or down, and does the average shrinkage increase or decrease? Then set the prior on tau to HalfNormal(0.1) — a strong belief that assays agree — by changing the -0.5 * t^2 term to -0.5 * (t / 0.1)^2, and describe what happens to the posterior means of the small assays.

8. Predictive checks

A posterior can be precise and wrong, because precision is a statement about the parameter within the model and says nothing about whether the model could have produced the data. The check is predictive: simulate datasets from the model and compare them with the real one.

  • A prior predictive check draws parameters from the prior and simulates data, before looking at the observations. It asks whether the priors imply anything absurd — pActivity values of 40, negative hit rates, potencies spanning twenty log units.
  • A posterior predictive check draws parameters from the posterior and simulates data, then compares a chosen summary of the simulations with the same summary of the real data[20].
kurtosis <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^4) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^2 - 3
skewness <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^1.5
set.seed(1)
prior_mu <- rnorm(400, 6.5, 2.0); prior_tau <- abs(rnorm(400, 0, 1)); prior_sig <- abs(rnorm(400, 0, 1))
prior_sim <- t(sapply(1:400, function(i)
  rnorm(50, prior_mu[i] + prior_tau[i] * rnorm(50), prior_sig[i])))
idx <- sample(nrow(post_h), 400)
post_sim <- t(sapply(idx, function(i) rnorm(length(yobs), theta_post[i, codes], sig_post[i])))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.6, 1), cex = 0.72)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 14), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "pActivity", ylab = "cumulative fraction",
     main = "prior predictive (grey) vs data")
for (i in 1:120) lines(sort(prior_sim[i, ]), seq(0, 1, length.out = 50), col = "#bbbbbb66", lwd = 0.5)
lines(sort(yobs), seq(0, 1, length.out = length(yobs)), col = PAL["orange"], lwd = 2)
plot(NA, xlim = c(2, 12), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "pActivity", ylab = "",
     main = "posterior predictive (blue) vs data")
for (i in 1:120) lines(sort(post_sim[i, ]), seq(0, 1, length.out = ncol(post_sim)),
                       col = adjustcolor(PAL["blue"], 0.25), lwd = 0.4)
lines(sort(yobs), seq(0, 1, length.out = length(yobs)), col = PAL["orange"], lwd = 2)
ks <- apply(post_sim, 1, kurtosis)
hist(ks, breaks = 40, col = "grey80", border = NA, xlim = range(c(ks, kurtosis(yobs))),
     xlab = "excess kurtosis of a simulated dataset", main = "a test statistic the model misses")
abline(v = kurtosis(yobs), col = PAL["orange"], lwd = 2)

par(op)
cat(sprintf("prior predictive: 2.5-97.5 %% range of simulated pActivity = [%.1f, %.1f] (data: [%.1f, %.1f])\n",
            quantile(prior_sim, 0.025), quantile(prior_sim, 0.975), min(yobs), max(yobs)))
## prior predictive: 2.5-97.5 % range of simulated pActivity = [1.7, 11.5] (data: [3.6, 9.8])
cat(sprintf("posterior predictive mean %.3f vs observed %.3f\n", mean(post_sim), mean(yobs)))
## posterior predictive mean 6.544 vs observed 6.545
cat(sprintf("posterior predictive SD   %.3f vs observed %.3f\n", sd(as.vector(post_sim)), sd(yobs)))
## posterior predictive SD   1.124 vs observed 1.125
cat(sprintf("observed excess kurtosis %.3f vs simulated %.3f [%.3f, %.3f]; posterior predictive p = %.4f\n",
            kurtosis(yobs), mean(ks), quantile(ks, 0.025), quantile(ks, 0.975), mean(ks <= kurtosis(yobs))))
## observed excess kurtosis -0.474 vs simulated -0.073 [-0.235, 0.079]; posterior predictive p = 0.0000
cat(sprintf("observed skewness %.3f (the model reproduces this one: p = %.3f)\n",
            skewness(yobs), mean(apply(post_sim, 1, skewness) >= skewness(yobs))))
## observed skewness 0.021 (the model reproduces this one: p = 0.882)
cat(sprintf("observed minimum %.2f vs simulated minima %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\n",
            min(yobs), mean(apply(post_sim, 1, min)),
            quantile(apply(post_sim, 1, min), 0.025), quantile(apply(post_sim, 1, min), 0.975)))
## observed minimum 3.57 vs simulated minima 2.74 [2.00, 3.27]

Figure 10. Predictive checks (orange: the observed data). Left: datasets simulated from the prior alone (grey) are far too broad — the priors permit pActivity values from below 2 to above 11 — which is acceptable for a weakly informative prior but would be a problem if they excluded the observed range. Centre: datasets simulated from the posterior (blue) track the observed distribution closely through the bulk, reproducing the mean to three decimals (6.545) and the standard deviation to three (1.125). Right: the model nevertheless fails one specific test — the excess kurtosis of the real data, −0.474, lies below every one of the 400 simulated values (simulated range −0.210 to +0.097, posterior predictive p = 0.000). The real potencies are lighter-tailed than a normal likelihood implies, because every assay is bounded by the concentration range it was run over; the simulated datasets contain compounds weaker (minimum 2.74 against the observed 3.57) and stronger than any real measurement.

The right-hand panel is the point of the exercise. A posterior predictive check is only as good as the summary statistic chosen, and the useful ones are those the model was not fitted to match. Means and standard deviations will almost always agree, because the model has parameters for them — and indeed they match to three decimals here. Skewness happens to pass as well (p = 0.88). Kurtosis, extreme quantiles, the number of zeros, or the autocorrelation of a time series are the statistics that reveal misfit, and one of them does. The honest conclusion for our model: it captures the centre, spread and asymmetry of the assay structure and gets the tails wrong, so posterior intervals for central quantities are trustworthy and predictions about extreme compounds are not.

9. The same model with lme4 — and what a probabilistic programming language would add

Writing samplers by hand is the right way to learn and the wrong way to work. The Python edition of this unit notes that its models are hand-written because the compiler behind PyMC[21][22] does not run on the build machine, and gives the PyMC code as text. The R edition has a better option for this particular model: lme4::lmer[2] fits the same hierarchical normal model by restricted maximum likelihood in one line, and comparing the two is the strongest available check on fifty lines of hand-written Metropolis-within-Gibbs.

dt_assay <- data.table(y = yobs, assay = factor(codes))
mm <- lmer(y ~ 1 + (1 | assay), data = dt_assay, REML = TRUE)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm))
blups <- coef(mm)$assay[, 1]
cat(sprintf("lmer   : intercept %.3f | between-assay SD %.3f | residual SD %.3f\n",
            fixef(mm)[1], vc$sdcor[1], vc$sdcor[2]))
## lmer   : intercept 6.747 | between-assay SD 0.836 | residual SD 0.828
cat(sprintf("Bayes  : mu        %.3f | tau            %.3f | sigma       %.3f\n",
            mean(mu_post), mean(tau_post), mean(sig_post)))
## Bayes  : mu        6.746 | tau            0.843 | sigma       0.828
cat(sprintf("correlation between lmer BLUPs and Bayesian posterior means: %.4f\n", cor(blups, theta_hat)))
## correlation between lmer BLUPs and Bayesian posterior means: 1.0000
cat(sprintf("mean |difference| between the two sets of 108 estimates: %.4f log units\n",
            mean(abs(blups - theta_hat))))
## mean |difference| between the two sets of 108 estimates: 0.0016 log units
cat(sprintf("largest |difference|: %.4f log units (assay %s, n = %d)\n",
            max(abs(blups - theta_hat)), assay_ids[which.max(abs(blups - theta_hat))],
            nj[which.max(abs(blups - theta_hat))]))
## largest |difference|: 0.0105 log units (assay CHEMBL4479774, n = 4)
p <- ggplot(data.table(blup = blups, bayes = theta_hat, n = nj, raw = ybar),
            aes(blup, bayes, size = n)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL["blue"], alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.6, 3), trans = "log10", name = "measurements") +
  labs(x = "lme4 conditional mode (BLUP) of the assay effect",
       y = "Bayesian posterior mean",
       title = "Two routes to partial pooling, 108 assays, one answer")
print(p)

Figure 11. The 108 assay estimates from the hand-written sampler against those from lmer, with point size proportional to assay size and the identity line dashed. The two agree to a correlation of 1.0000, a mean absolute difference of 0.0016 log units and a worst case of about 0.01 — far below the Monte-Carlo noise of the sampler, and three orders of magnitude below the between-assay standard deviation. The variance components agree too: between-assay 0.836 (lmer) against 0.843 (Bayes), within-assay 0.828 against 0.828. The small systematic gap in the between-assay term is expected: REML returns a point estimate of τ, while the Bayesian posterior mean averages over the uncertainty in τ, which is asymmetric and therefore slightly larger.

This agreement is worth dwelling on, because it tells a student which tool to reach for. For a balanced-ish hierarchical normal model with no further structure, lmer gives the same partial pooling in one line and in a fraction of a second, with the empirical-Bayes conditional modes that genomics calls shrinkage estimates. What it does not give is a distribution: there is no posterior for τ, no probability that one assay exceeds another, no predictive interval for an unrun assay, and the uncertainty in the variance components is not propagated into the group estimates. Those are the four things §7 produced by counting draws, and they are the reason to pay the extra cost when the question needs them.

For models beyond this one — non-normal likelihoods, censored potencies, several nested levels, a hierarchical regression with varying slopes — the right tool is a probabilistic programming language rather than either of these. In R that is brms[32] or rstanarm, both front-ends to Stan[23], in which this unit’s model is one line of formula syntax:

## Not run here: brms/rstanarm require a Stan toolchain, which this build environment lacks.
## In a Colab R runtime, install the brms package once, then:
library(brms)
fit <- brm(y ~ 1 + (1 | assay), data = dt_assay,
           prior = c(prior(normal(6.5, 2), class = "Intercept"),
                     prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd"),        ## HalfNormal(1) on tau
                     prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sigma")),    ## HalfNormal(1) on sigma
           chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 0)
summary(fit)                 ## posterior means, 95 % CrI, R-hat and ESS for every parameter
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 100)  ## the posterior predictive check of section 8, in one call

Substitution in the R edition — no probabilistic programming language

The chunk above is shown but not evaluated (eval = FALSE): brms and rstanarm need a working C++ toolchain and a compiled Stan backend, which the environment this unit is knitted in does not provide. Everything in this unit therefore runs on base R, and the hand-written sampler of §7 is validated against lme4 in Figure 11 rather than against Stan. This is in any case the better teaching path — if you cannot write a Metropolis sampler, you cannot diagnose one — and the code above runs unchanged in Colab once the brms package has been installed there. Two details of it are worth copying: brms uses the non-centred parameterisation internally (sampling standard normals and transforming, rather than sampling the group effects directly), which avoids the funnel-shaped geometry that makes hierarchical models hard to sample, and summary() reports R-hat and effective sample size automatically, which is the main practical reason to use it.

Priors for variance parameters deserve one specific remark, because the default choice in older textbooks is bad: an inverse-gamma prior with tiny parameters is not “uninformative” for a between-group standard deviation and can dominate the posterior when the number of groups is small. A half-normal or half-Cauchy on the standard deviation itself, as used in §7 and in the brms block above, is the modern default[24][25].

10. Credible intervals and confidence intervals

The two are different objects that often look the same.

  • A 95 % credible interval contains the parameter with probability 0.95 given the data and the model. It is a statement about the parameter.
  • A 95 % confidence interval is produced by a procedure that, over hypothetical repetitions of the experiment, contains the true value 95 % of the time. It is a statement about the procedure, and the interval in front of you either contains the parameter or does not[26].

With plenty of data and a weak prior the two nearly coincide, which is why the misinterpretation of confidence intervals is so persistent[27]. They separate when data are scarce or the parameter is near a boundary.

cmp_int <- rbindlist(lapply(list(c(40, k_active), c(400, k400), c(12, 0)), function(z) {
  n_ <- z[1]; k_ <- z[2]; ph <- k_ / n_
  wald <- ph + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n_)
  wilson <- as.numeric(prop.test(k_, n_, correct = FALSE)$conf.int)
  data.table(n = n_, k = k_, MLE = ph,
             Wald = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", wald[1], wald[2]),
             Wilson = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", wilson[1], wilson[2]),
             Bayes_mean = (a0 + k_) / (a0 + b0 + n_),
             credible = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", qbeta(0.025, a0 + k_, b0 + n_ - k_),
                                qbeta(0.975, a0 + k_, b0 + n_ - k_)),
             w_lo = wilson[1], w_hi = wilson[2],
             c_lo = qbeta(0.025, a0 + k_, b0 + n_ - k_), c_hi = qbeta(0.975, a0 + k_, b0 + n_ - k_))
}))
plot_dt <- rbind(cmp_int[, .(lab = sprintf("n=%d, k=%d", n, k), est = MLE, lo = w_lo, hi = w_hi,
                             kind = "Wilson confidence interval")],
                 cmp_int[, .(lab = sprintf("n=%d, k=%d", n, k), est = Bayes_mean, lo = c_lo, hi = c_hi,
                             kind = "Bayesian credible interval")])
p <- ggplot(plot_dt, aes(est, lab, colour = kind)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.18, position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("orange", "blue")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "hit rate", y = NULL, title = "The two intervals agree until the data run out")
print(p)

knitr::kable(cmp_int[, .(n, k, MLE, Wald, Wilson, Bayes_mean, credible)], digits = 3)
n k MLE Wald Wilson Bayes_mean credible
40 6 0.150 [0.039, 0.261] [0.071, 0.291] 0.133 [0.060, 0.229]
400 37 0.092 [0.064, 0.121] [0.068, 0.125] 0.093 [0.067, 0.122]
12 0 0.000 [0.000, 0.000] [0.000, 0.242] 0.062 [0.008, 0.167]

Figure 12. Wilson confidence intervals (orange) and Bayesian credible intervals under the Beta(2,18) prior (blue) for three datasets. At n = 400 they are nearly identical ([0.068, 0.125] against [0.067, 0.122]). At n = 40 they differ by a few hundredths and tell the same story. At n = 12 with zero actives they separate decisively: the maximum-likelihood estimate is exactly 0, the Wald interval collapses to the degenerate [0.000, 0.000] — a statement no one believes — the Wilson interval runs to 0.242, and the credible interval is [0.008, 0.167] with a posterior mean of 0.062, which is what a chemist would actually say after twelve failures.

The boundary case in the table is the practical argument for Bayesian intervals in small-sample work. “Zero of twelve” is extremely common in early screening, in toxicity studies and in rare-event clinical data, and the classical machinery handles it badly without corrections — in R, prop.test gives the Wilson interval and binom.test the Clopper–Pearson one, both of which behave sensibly, while the textbook Wald formula does not. A weakly informative prior solves it by construction.

Which to report

Report the one whose definition matches the sentence you want to write. If the sentence is “there is a 95 % probability that the hit rate is between 6 % and 23 %”, you need a credible interval, and you must state the prior. If the sentence is “a procedure with 95 % long-run coverage gives [7 %, 29 %]”, a confidence interval suffices. What is never acceptable is to compute one and describe it as the other[27].

11. Model comparison: Bayes factors and information criteria, briefly

A Bayes factor is the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two models, \(BF_{12}=P(D\mid M_1)/P(D\mid M_2)\): how much the data shift the relative odds of the two models[28]. It is attractive because it can support the null hypothesis rather than merely failing to reject it[29], and dangerous because the marginal likelihood depends on the priors even when the posterior does not — a prior ten times too wide divides the Bayes factor by roughly ten. Computing it requires integrating over the whole prior, which is hard in more than a few dimensions.

Information criteria (AIC and BIC, Unit 9) approximate related quantities much more cheaply, and the modern Bayesian default for predictive comparison is cross-validated predictive density rather than either. For this course the practical rule is: use posterior distributions to answer questions about parameters, use cross-validation (Unit 12) to compare predictive models, and reach for Bayes factors only with explicit, justified priors and a sensitivity analysis.

marginal_likelihood <- function(a, b, n, k, grid_n = 20000) {
  t <- seq(1e-6, 1 - 1e-6, length.out = grid_n)
  sum(dbeta(t, a, b) * dbinom(k, n, t)) * diff(t)[1]
}
m_point <- dbinom(k_active, n_tested, 0.10)        ## M2: the hit rate is exactly 10 %
bf <- rbindlist(lapply(list(c(2, 18), c(1, 9), c(20, 180), c(1, 1)), function(pp) {
  data.table(prior = sprintf("Beta(%.1f, %.1f)", pp[1], pp[2]),
             prior_sd = sqrt(pp[1] * pp[2] / (sum(pp)^2 * (sum(pp) + 1))),
             BF_flexible_vs_point = marginal_likelihood(pp[1], pp[2], n_tested, k_active) / m_point,
             posterior_mean = (pp[1] + k_active) / (sum(pp) + n_tested))
}))
cat("the data are identical in every row; only the prior width changed.\n")
## the data are identical in every row; only the prior width changed.
knitr::kable(bf, digits = 4)
prior prior_sd BF_flexible_vs_point posterior_mean
Beta(2.0, 18.0) 0.0655 0.6932 0.1333
Beta(1.0, 9.0) 0.0905 0.5381 0.1400
Beta(20.0, 180.0) 0.0212 0.9636 0.1083
Beta(1.0, 1.0) 0.2887 0.2285 0.1667

The table makes the warning concrete: the four priors give posterior means spanning 0.058 (0.108 to 0.167), yet their Bayes factors span a factor of four (0.228 to 0.964), because a wider prior spreads its marginal likelihood over possibilities the data rule out. Note also that every Bayes factor here is below 1, i.e. the data mildly favour the point hypothesis “the rate is exactly 10 %” over the flexible model — unsurprising with 6 active of 40, but a conclusion whose strength depends on a prior the point model does not have. Posterior summaries are robust to the prior here; the Bayes factor is not. That asymmetry is the reason this course teaches estimation rather than Bayesian hypothesis testing.

Bridge

This unit is the Bayesian counterpart of the block that preceded it: Unit 7’s confidence intervals become credible intervals in §10, Unit 8’s p-values become posterior probabilities in §2 and §11, and Unit 9’s blocking factor and its lmer fit become the hierarchical model of §7, cross-checked against lmer in §9. The Python counterpart of this unit is here and the R edition is indexed at the course root. Forward, the base-rate arithmetic of §2 is the foundation of Unit 19’s enrichment metrics, the partial pooling of §7 is how Unit 20 should combine replica averages, Unit 17 builds distribution-free prediction intervals as the non-Bayesian route to the same goal, and Unit 21 uses the empirical-Bayes shrinkage of gene-wise variances that §7 motivates. In the sister courses, the bioinformatics unit on molecular docking produces the ranked lists whose hit probability §2 computes, the cheminformatics unit on chemical databases explains where the 108 assays of §7 come from, and the R edition of the AI course, indexed here, covers naive Bayes and probabilistic classifiers.

12. Summary

You should be able to explain, without notes:

  • Bayes’ theorem in words, and why the posterior requires a prior as well as a likelihood;
  • the base-rate fallacy, and why a screen with an enrichment factor of 8 on a 0.1 %-active library still delivers 99 inactive compounds in every 100 ordered;
  • conjugate updating for the beta–binomial — prior Beta(2,18) plus 6 of 40 gives Beta(8,52), mean 0.1333 — and that the posterior mean is a weighted compromise between prior and data;
  • how to compute a posterior by grid approximation, and the dimensional limit that makes it fail;
  • how a Metropolis sampler works, why the normalising constant cancels, and the three diagnostics (acceptance rate, R-hat, effective sample size) that separated a healthy chain from one with 17 effective draws;
  • what partial pooling does, why small assays shrank by 0.151 log units and large ones by 0.008, and which of the group’s data structures are hierarchical;
  • that lmer reproduces the same 108 partially pooled estimates to a correlation of 1.0000, and what it does not give;
  • what prior and posterior predictive checks test, and why the useful test statistic (kurtosis, p = 0.000) is one the model was not fitted to match;
  • the difference between a credible and a confidence interval, and the zero-of-twelve case where Wald gives [0, 0] and the credible interval gives [0.008, 0.167];
  • why posterior summaries are usually robust to the prior while Bayes factors moved by a factor of four over the same four priors;
  • how to report a Bayesian analysis: model, priors, sampler diagnostics, posterior summaries, prior sensitivity, predictive check.

13. Self-assessment

  1. A test with 99 % sensitivity and 95 % specificity is positive. Why might you still be unlikely to be ill?
Because the posterior depends on the prior prevalence. With a disease frequency of 1 in 1,000, the 5 % false-positive rate applied to the 99.9 % healthy majority produces about fifty times more false positives than true positives, giving P(ill | positive) = 99/5,094 ≈ 1.9 %.
  1. Your virtual screen has EF(1 %) = 20 on a library whose prevalence of actives is 0.05 %. You order 50 compounds. How many actives do you expect?
P(active | selected) ≈ 20 × 0.0005 = 0.01, so about 0.5 actives among 50 compounds. This is the arithmetic behind “order a hundred, not five”, and the reason an experimental collaborator asks how many compounds the screen is confident about.
  1. Prior Beta(2,18), data 6 active of 40. What is the posterior and its mean?
Beta(2+6, 18+34) = Beta(8, 52), with mean 8/60 = 0.1333 — between the prior mean of 0.10 and the data estimate of 0.15, closer to the data because 40 observations outweigh 20 observations’ worth of prior. Its 95 % credible interval is [0.060, 0.229].
  1. Why does the normalising constant not matter in the Metropolis algorithm?
Because the accept/reject decision depends only on the ratio of posterior densities at two points, and the unknown constant P(D) appears in both numerator and denominator. This is what makes MCMC possible for models whose evidence integral cannot be computed — and it is why the sampler in §6 needs only dbeta(…, log = TRUE) + dbinom(…, log = TRUE).
  1. Your chain has an acceptance rate of 0.97. Is that good?
No — it means the proposal steps are far too small, so the chain crawls and consecutive draws are nearly identical. In §6 that chain had an effective sample size of 17 per chain against 687 for the well-tuned one, and R-hat 1.060, even though its posterior mean was correct to three decimals. For a random-walk Metropolis sampler, aim for roughly 0.2–0.5 and check R-hat and ESS rather than the trace alone.
  1. What is R-hat and what value is acceptable?
The ratio of an estimate of the total posterior variance (pooling chains) to the within-chain variance; if chains started from different places have converged to the same distribution it approaches 1. Values above about 1.01 indicate that the chains have not mixed, and the posterior summaries should not be used.
  1. An assay with three compounds has a mean pActivity of 7.97; the hierarchical model reports 7.67. Has the model thrown away information?
No — it has combined the three measurements with the information that assays in this dataset are distributed around 6.75 with a between-assay SD of 0.84. A mean of 7.97 from three measurements is weak evidence of an exceptional assay and strong evidence of a small sample. The shrunken estimate is the better prediction for the next compound in that assay, as the held-out test of §7.1 confirms (RMSE 0.959 against 0.995 for assays with n ≤ 5).
  1. When does shrinkage not happen?
When the group has enough data for its own mean to be precise (λ → 1 as n grows; it reached 0.998 for the 501-compound assay), or when the between-group variance tau is large relative to the within-group variance, meaning the groups really are different and pooling would be wrong. The model estimates tau from the data rather than assuming it, which is the point.
  1. Your posterior predictive check shows the model reproduces the mean and SD but not the kurtosis. What now?
Report it, and decide whether it matters for the question. The model has parameters for the mean and the variance, so matching those is not evidence; the failure on kurtosis (observed −0.474, simulated −0.210 to +0.097) says the normal likelihood is wrong in the tails. If the conclusion concerns central quantities it stands; if it concerns extreme compounds, use a heavier-tailed likelihood such as Student’s t.
  1. Twelve compounds tested, none active. What do you report?
Not “the hit rate is 0”. Report a credible interval under a stated prior — [0.008, 0.167] under Beta(2,18) — or a Wilson confidence interval ([0.000, 0.242] from prop.test), and state explicitly that zero of twelve is compatible with a hit rate of 10 %. The Wald interval of [0, 0] is an artefact of the formula.
  1. Why are posterior means robust to the prior here while Bayes factors are not?
Because the posterior renormalises over the parameter space and the likelihood dominates once there are enough data, whereas the marginal likelihood integrates the likelihood against the prior, so a wider prior dilutes it. In §11 four priors moved the posterior mean by 0.058 and the Bayes factor by a factor of four.
  1. A referee objects that your prior is subjective. What is the answer?
That every modelling choice is, and that this one is written down. Show the prior predictive check, show the sensitivity table across several defensible priors (§5), and show that the conclusion is unchanged — or, if it changes, say so, because then the data are not sufficient to support it without the prior. For the hierarchical model you can add the strongest check of all: lmer, which uses no prior at all, gives the same 108 estimates.

Glossary

Base-rate fallacy
Ignoring the prior prevalence when interpreting a positive test or a predicted hit.
Bayes factor
Ratio of two models’ marginal likelihoods; sensitive to the priors even when posteriors are not.
BLUP / conditional mode
The mixed-model point estimate of a group effect; the frequentist analogue of a posterior mean under partial pooling.
Conjugate prior
A prior whose family is preserved by the update, making the posterior available in closed form (beta–binomial, normal–normal).
Credible interval
An interval containing the parameter with a stated posterior probability, given data, model and prior.
Effective sample size
The number of independent draws an autocorrelated chain is worth.
Enrichment factor
Hit rate among the selected fraction divided by the library prevalence; capped at 1/prevalence.
Grid approximation
Evaluating prior × likelihood on a grid and normalising; exact in one or two dimensions, hopeless beyond three.
Hierarchical model
A model in which group parameters are themselves draws from a common distribution, producing partial pooling.
Likelihood
The probability of the observed data as a function of the parameters.
Marginal likelihood (evidence)
The probability of the data averaged over the prior; the denominator of Bayes’ theorem.
MCMC
Markov chain Monte Carlo: a random walk whose stationary distribution is the posterior.
Metropolis algorithm
Propose, compute the density ratio, accept with probability min(1, r); the ancestor of all MCMC.
Metropolis-within-Gibbs
Conjugate (Gibbs) draws for the parameters that allow them, Metropolis steps for the rest; the sampler of §7.
Non-centred parameterisation
Sampling a standard normal and transforming, to avoid the funnel geometry of hierarchical posteriors.
Partial pooling
Estimating a group parameter as a compromise between its own data and the overall distribution.
Posterior
The distribution of the parameters given the data; the output of a Bayesian analysis.
Posterior predictive check
Simulating datasets from the posterior and comparing a summary with the observed data.
Prior
The distribution of the parameters before seeing the data; an assumption to be stated and varied.
R-hat
Convergence diagnostic comparing between-chain and within-chain variance; should be below about 1.01.
Shrinkage
Movement of a group’s estimate towards the overall mean, by an amount decreasing with the group’s sample size.
Weakly informative prior
A prior that excludes absurd values without determining the answer; the practical default.
